newsitem.title: YUGOSLAVIA: Serbian parliament approves new government.
newsitem.headline: Serbian parliament approves new government.

text.p: The Serbian parliament approved a new cabinet on Tuesday as embattled President Slobodan Milosevic sought to shore up his power base after months of civil unrest.
Among the key changes was the appointment of Milan Beko to head a new ministry that will begin the privatisation of the huge and financially ailing state sector of the economy.

Deputy prime minister Slobodan Babic was ousted, along with six other ministers. Milutin Stojkovic was named to replace Babic and Beko was appointed along with 11 other new ministers, three of them without portfolio.

One ministry was abolished and three were created. Radmila Milentijevic, a hardline Milosevic loyalist, was appointed to the information ministry post vacant since December 6 when Aleksandar Tijanic resigned.

Political and economic analysts and members of the Zajedno (Together) coalition, which forced Milosevic to concede opposition victories in November municipal elections, dismissed the appointments, saying many of them were non-entities.
"All the newly elected ministers are anonymous persons, but such a move by the government could have been expected," an economic expert said.

"...This new privatisation ministry is planned to create an impression that privatisation in Serbia is going ahead (because)...the current regime lacks $110 million per month to pay wages, salaries and cover its costs," the economist said.
Kosta Obradovic, spokesman for the Civic Alliance party which is a member of Zajedno, said there was no official party reaction but the appointments were mostly political unknowns.
"The only names known to me on the list are Radmila Milentijevic and Bratislava Morina (Minister of Family Affairs)," Obradovic said.

"I cannot explain this choice but nothing the regime has been doing, especially after November 17, makes much sense," Obradovic said, referring to the date of the municipal elections in which the government annulled Zajedno victories, touching off three months of street protests.

"I do not know why there was a change in the government, why the old persons have 'sinned' and why these anonymous persons have been put in their place. I do not know what they did to merit being chosen for the government."
The new appointees were sworn in immediately after the 250-member parliament, with 157 present, voted 130 for and 25 against, with two abstentions.
